column2: Most big losses come from three things: buying when everyone is excited, selling when everyone is scared, and putting in money you’ll need soon.
Following the crowd (buy queues, Telegram signals): only buy with a Codal file and your own numbers.
Clinging to the purchase price: “I’ll wait until it gets back to what I paid.” Ask: “If I didn’t own this share today, would I buy it?”
Reading only good news about your own share: write down the best argument against it too.
At a crowded sale, people buy things they don’t need just because everyone else is buying.
Mental mistakes that burn money
Falls and recoveries aren’t symmetrical: a 50% fall needs a 100% rise to recover; an 80% fall, 400%.
Iran’s market has seen big, multi-year falls, such as after the 1399 peak.
Assume from the start that one day you’ll live through a 40 to 50% fall.
If 100 million halves and 50 is left, to get back to 100 it has to double, not just grow 50%.

When the market falls, first ask: “Has the company’s lasting profit changed, or only its price?” If only the price, it may be an opportunity, and you carry out the step-by-step buying plan you wrote in advance.
When the market is hot, recalculate how many years until you get your money back. When everyone says “this time is different”, go back to your plan’s weights.
The 48-hour rule: put off any buy or sell outside your plan by at least 48 hours.
If you’re angry, don’t send the message you wrote until tomorrow; emotional buying and selling is the same.
The risk of ruin means losing so much that you can’t carry on. In Iran three roads lead there:
1. Loans and broker credit to buy shares; with a sell queue you may not be able to get out. FIS doesn’t borrow.
2. Putting half your money in one share or one industry.
3. Putting in money you’ll need in the next 1 to 2 years.
A swimmer who goes into deep water with a heavy bag drowns in a small wave; a loan for shares is that heavy bag.
A loss that ends the game
If you have 1 billion tomans in shares and the cap per company is 10%, at most 100 million in each company.
If the worst reasonable event for that company is a 60% fall, your total money only falls 6%; that’s bearable.
For riskier companies, halve the cap.
According to Dr. Khosravani, if an amount scares you, cut it down until it no longer matters to you.
If one of a home’s 10 rooms catches fire, the house still stands; if everything is in one room, it doesn’t.
Dr. Khosravani gives an example: if even 6 million tomans stresses you, trade with 3 million.
According to him you can’t control feelings, but you can control the behaviour that comes after them. A smaller amount makes that easier.
The 10% cap per company is a ceiling, not a target. If you’re not calm even with that, lower it.
You learn to drive on a quiet street, not the motorway; once you’re calm, you speed up.
Each buy and sell costs about 1% in fees and tax. If you buy and sell every week, more than half your capital goes on fees in a year.
The main FIS return comes from the company’s profit growth and each year’s dividends; you only get that by holding.
Instead of “Should I sell now?”, each quarter ask “Is the reason I bought still there?”
If you moved house every month, agents’ fees and removals would eat all your savings.
Set a fixed time: once a week, say Thursday, and the second week of each month for monthly reports.
Update the company’s numbers first, then look at the chart and price.
Write in a journal: the date, what you did, why, what number would change your mind, and your mood (1 to 5).
Leave signal channels and turn off price alerts.
Someone on a diet doesn’t keep sweets in the fridge; a long-term investor doesn’t keep price alerts on.
Financial intelligence means the skill of solving money problems, not how much income you have.
Its most important skill is prioritising: is your main problem low income or high spending?
The first investment is in yourself: skills and financial logic. The tools are simple: a calculator, a laptop and logic.
If you come up short every month, the answer may not be a second job; it may be subscriptions and small daily purchases.
“The Goldun Law” is a book and course of his about living in harmony with the laws of nature. The first three laws:
1. Don’t compare yourself with others; your measure is yesterday’s you.
2. “Find your soil”: like a plant in a pot, find the place and work where you grow.
3. Know your needs. A money goal that comes from a real need lasts; one that comes from keeping up with others pulls you into a lot of risk.
Someone who buys a new car with a loan because a colleague bought one didn’t spend for their own need; they spent for comparison.
The outline of the “Goldun Law” course has 22 laws; their titles are in the table.
This app only explains the first three laws, from his public videos; the rest are in the book and the course.
Like a book’s table of contents: you see the chapter titles, but you have to read each chapter in the book itself.
A story he tells in his channel: a farmer who never sows for fear of rain and pests. Someone who does nothing out of fear loses the most.
The answer to fear isn’t recklessness; it’s a plan: start small, practise with pretend money, have a cap per share and rainy-day money.
Time is the most important factor in compounding; but always measure the return after inflation.
Someone who never learns to swim for fear of drowning is in more danger than someone who practises in the shallow end.
“Is knowledge better, or wealth?” is the name of one of his talks. It has two clear conclusions:
Wealth comes from creating value for many people, meaning meeting more people’s needs; and its higher aim is spiritual wealth.
Write your own answer to “work you love, or work that pays?” in your journal, then see his answer in the same video.
Someone who wins the lottery but can’t manage money is usually back where they started a few years later.
In his view your most important asset is you: knowledge and reading make your world, and so your assets, bigger.
Money spent learning a skill pays off years later too; like a tree planted once that bears fruit every year.
